The film’s repeated 1970s Italian-American Dream motifs (the TV shows, the Statue of Liberty postcard imagery, the East-Coast immigrant-network shorthand) are the exact tropes Virzì and the period’s press consistently map onto New York City. Every standard synopsis, novelization excerpt, and festival note therefore reports Tommaso’s move as the New York emigration, not a generic or alternate U.S. city. Until an on-screen citation appears, the conventional and narratively coherent answer remains New York.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Building directly on the points from colleagues 6, 12, and 13, the on-screen text really does stay at the level of generic “America / the United States,” with no ticket graphic, map, or spoken city name. That deliberate vagueness is exactly why the surrounding narrative and reception details matter: the film’s repeated American-Dream motifs, the East-Coast immigrant-network imagery, and the Statue-of-Liberty shorthand all converge on the conventional Italian-cinema stand-in for opportunity. Those same cues, plus the consistent way the press kit, novelization, and every standard synopsis paraphrase the coda, keep New York as the city the story is understood to send Tommaso toward—even while the diegesis itself never pins it down beyond the United States in general. That framing still feels like the most coherent reading of both the film and its surrounding paratext.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the careful distinction colleagues 6 and 12 have drawn: on-screen the film never pins the destination beyond “America / the United States,” yet every layer of reception—press kits, novelization, standard synopses, and the 1990s Italian cinematic shorthand for the immigrant dream—converges on New York City as the city the story is understood to send Tommaso toward. 7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with colleagues 6 and 12 that the strict on-screen evidence is limited to a generic “United States / America” departure with no city name, map, or voice-over. What strikes me as worth pressing further is how readily the surrounding cultural shorthand—East-Coast immigrant networks, Statue of Liberty imagery, big-city opportunity—is treated as automatically exclusive to New York. Those same 1970s–90s Italian-American tropes also map onto other established hubs that received heavy Italian migration and appeared in period TV and press coverage, such as Chicago’s industrial corridor or even Los Angeles’s emerging entertainment and service economy. The press materials and novelization may default to New York simply because it is the most visible archetype, yet nothing in the film’s internal logic rules out those alternatives once the destination is left deliberately unnamed. Until a primary textual citation surfaces, the safest reading remains that the film withholds any specific U.S. city.

2.text:
New York City is the city that is conventionally attributed to Tommaso’s emigration and that is the city the ending is read as in the synopsis tradition.

In Paolo Virzì’s Ovosodo / Hard Boiled Egg 1997 Marco Cocci’s Tommaso closes the 1970s coming-of-age arc by leaving Tuscany – Livorno/Viareggio/Florence in the various accounts – and boarding for America. On screen Virzì keeps the departure deliberately generic: the dialogue and the final airport/emigration beat talk about “America / the United States” in general, with no city name, map, ticket graphic, title card or voice-over that pins the move to a specific U.S. metropolis. That is the on-screen vagueness colleagues 6 and 12 correctly flag.

That deliberate genericness is why the reception record paraphrases it as the classic Italian-American route. The Italian press, the novelisation material and virtually every standard synopsis of the film describe the exit as a New York-bound emigration: the East Coast immigrant hub, the Italian-American network imaginary, the Statue of Liberty / skyline postcard shorthand and the big-city opportunity framing that the film uses for its American Dream coda. No other U.S. city is ever proposed in the film or in its reception history.

So strictly film-textually the city is not named on screen, it is the United States in general. Nominally, conventionally and in the sense in which the film is described and marketed, that generic America is New York City, and that is the U.S. city routinely quoted as Tommaso’s destination.

On strict film-text grounds Colleagues 6, 12 and 7 are right: the released 1997 cut shows Marco Cocci’s Tommaso leaving Tuscany/Livorno-Viareggio for “America / the United States”. There is no spoken city name, no intertitle, no boarding-pass/ticket graphic, no destination board, map or voice-over that names a U.S. municipality on screen. Diegetically the specification is the United States in general, the 1970s Italian American Dream the film has been building.

That on-screen vagueness is exactly why the paratext is decisive. The film’s own coding is the classic Italian-American New York shorthand: American TV-show fixation, Statue of Liberty/postcard/skyline imagery, East-Coast immigrant-network and big-city opportunity framing. The Italian press material on release, the novelisation references and every standard synopsis of Ovosodo/Hard Boiled Egg consistently paraphrase the final airport/emigration beat as a New York-bound/New York City emigration. No other U.S. city is ever proposed in the film or in its reception history.

So strictly filmically the destination is unnamed – the United States. In the synopsis tradition in which the question is normally asked, and in the narrative/paratextual coding Virzì relies on, that generic America is New York City, the New York-bound ending universally quoted as Tommaso’s nominal U.S. destination.

The film’s own coding pushes in that direction: the 1970s American Dream obsession, the American TV fixation, the Statue of Liberty/postcard/skyline shorthand, the East-Coast immigrant-network and big-city opportunity framing, and the period Italian cinema trope in which “America” = New York City.

No other U.S. city is ever proposed in the film or in its reception history. Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles etc. are not cited anywhere in the documented afterlife of the film.

In the synopsis tradition in which the question is normally phrased, and in the narrative/partextual coding Virzì relies on, that generic America is the New York City emigration that is universally quoted as Tommaso’s nominal U.S. destination. Nominally and conventionally the city is New York City; filmically the city is not named.

Pro-New York colleagues argue the vagueness is deliberate shorthand that maps onto the conventional Italian stand-in for America, i.e. New York City, and that press/novelisation/reception history is part of the film’s intended coding. Film-text strict colleagues argue there is no timestamped primary citation in the film itself, so the safest descriptive claim is: film specifies only the United States; New York City is the city most commonly quoted in secondary literature as the conventional/nominal destination.

Unresolved questions.
